paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair is a RASopathy. Its features resemble Noonan syndrome, and it also has distinctive ectodermal abnormalities (Mazzanti et al., 2003; Motta et al., 2019). Mazzanti et al. (2003) described affected children with short stature, macrocephaly, a short neck with redundant skin, severe growth hormone (GH) deficiency, mild psychomotor delay with attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), darkly pigmented hairless skin, and loose anagen hair. In a larger series of mutation-positive individuals, Cordeddu et al. (2009) also noted cardiac anomalies, with mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects overrepresented, and a hypernasal voice.

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1991) reported a 4.5-year-old girl with Noonan syndrome and loose anagen hair. Her hair was short and blond, was easily pluckable, and had never been cut. Scalp biopsy showed marked cleft formation between fragmented inner root sheaths and irregularly shaped hair shafts.

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1997) reviewed 19 patients with loose anagen hair (14 children and 5 adults, aged 8 months to 47 years). Associated conditions were Noonan syndrome in a 5-year-old boy and alopecia areata in a 3-year-old boy. In all cases, a trichogram showed a predominance of anagen hairs (80 to 100%) without sheaths. Pathologic study of hair from 5 patients showed no morphologic abnormalities of the hair follicles apart from a high incidence of fragmentation of the inner root sheath. The authors concluded that the pathologic findings had no specific features and were of little diagnostic value.

paragraphs.text: Mazzanti et al. (2003) described 3 children who shared the same facial phenotype. All had short stature, macrocephaly, enlarged cerebrospinal fluid spaces, a short neck with redundant skin, severe GH deficiency, and mild psychomotor delay with ADHD. Two of the 3 had mild dilatation of the pulmonary root. The children also had a unique combination of ectodermal abnormalities: darkly pigmented, hairless skin and hair of an unusual appearance defined as loose anagen hair. The authors noted that the children's appearance was not completely typical of Noonan syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that 25 individuals carrying the SHOC2 S2G mutation had a relatively consistent phenotype. Their facial features looked typical of Noonan syndrome and included macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, palpebral ptosis, and low-set, posteriorly rotated ears. Common features also included a short, webbed neck and pectus anomalies. Patients had reduced growth, often with proven GH deficiency, as well as cognitive deficits and distinctive hyperactive behavior that improved with age in most. Their hair was easily pluckable, sparse, thin, and slow-growing. In 12 patients, loose anagen hair was confirmed by microscopic examination of pulled hairs. Most had darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis. Most also had cardiac anomalies, and mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects were significantly overrepresented compared with the general Noonan syndrome population. The voice was characteristically hypernasal. In several patients, the referring pediatricians had thought that the newborn or young infant had features suggestive of Costello syndrome or cardiofaciocutaneous (CFC) syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with the SHOC2 S2G mutation. Fetal distress required premature delivery at 32 weeks. After birth he had dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress. Echocardiography showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The cardiac lesion progressed rapidly, and he was discharged home for palliative care. The authors noted that his cardiac findings and other features were not typical of previously reported individuals with this mutation and expanded the clinical phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 male patients with the SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly mutation. All had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse light-colored hair, increased fine wrinkles, ligamentous laxity, and developmental delay. All 4 who were assessed had a structural cardiac anomaly. Four of the 5 had hypotonia and macrocephaly. Three of the 5 had polyhydramnios, increased birth weight, or needed a feeding tube. None was formally diagnosed with loose anagen hair, but all had sparse, very slow-growing hair with an unruly texture and unusually light color, as well as unusually long eyelashes. Four of the 5 patients had been suspected of having Costello syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Patient 1 of Gripp et al. (2013) was born by cesarean section at 38 weeks for macrosomia after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios and a third-trimester cystic hygroma. He had pyloric stenosis that required surgical repair. Severe failure to thrive led to gastrostomy tube placement at 5 months. He also had mild pulmonic valve stenosis, low axial tone, and motor delay. At 2 4/12 years his OFC was 54.3 cm (+3 SD). He had sparse, very fine hair, ptosis, downslanting palpebral fissures, a short neck, hepatosplenomegaly, hemangiomas, and numerous fine wrinkles on the hands. Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia was suspected at 2 3/12 years, but the bone marrow findings were most consistent with primary myelofibrosis. Bone marrow DNA was negative for the JAK2 V617F mutation. He died at 2.5 years after splenectomy in preparation for bone marrow transplantation. The authors described this as the first hematologic neoplasm in a patient with a SHOC2 mutation. Because the JAK2 mutation was absent, they suggested that the SHOC2 mutation may have predisposed to the myelofibrosis.

These were relative megalencephaly with enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, and a relatively small posterior fossa indicated by a vertical tentorium, which was seen in all 4 patients assessed. paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) selected SHOC2 as the best candidate gene using in silico protein network analysis seeded with known mutant RAS-MAPK proteins. They sequenced SHOC2 in 96 individuals with Noonan syndrome who were negative for mutations in known disease genes. In 4 unrelated individuals they found a heterozygous 4A-G transition in the SHOC2 gene, predicting a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution. All 4 cases were sporadic. In the 3 with parental DNA available, the parents did not carry the change and paternity was confirmed, indicating de novo occurrence. The mutation was present in DNA from several tissues, consistent with germline transmission. The authors then analyzed SHOC2 in 410 mutation-negative individuals with Noonan syndrome or a related phenotype. They found the same 4A-G change in 21 of them and showed that it was de novo in the 12 families with parental DNA available. No other disease-associated SHOC2 variant was identified in the cohort. In functional studies, the S2G mutation introduced an N-myristoylation site, which caused aberrant targeting of SHOC2 to the plasma membrane and impaired its translocation to the nucleus after growth factor stimulation.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) showed that the S2G substitution makes SHOC2 a substrate for N-myristoyltransferase (NMT). In Cos-1 cells, SHOC2 S2G incorporated [3H]-myristic acid, whereas wildtype SHOC2 and the disease-unrelated S2A mutant did not. Wildtype SHOC2 was distributed through the cytoplasm and nucleus in starved cells and was restricted to the nucleus after EGF stimulation. In contrast, S2G was targeted to the cell membrane in both conditions. The NMT inhibitor 2-hydroxymyristic acid reduced or abolished this membrane localization. Even without efficient myristoylation, the mutant did not translocate to the nucleus. Wildtype and S2G SHOC2 did not heterodimerize, which ruled out a dominant-negative effect through sequestration of the wildtype protein. S2G increased EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation compared with wildtype in Neuro2A cells, but not significantly in Cos-1 or 293T cells. The authors concluded that acquired N-myristoylation leads to constitutive membrane targeting and to cell context-specific increases in MAPK activation. They also proposed that loose anagen hair reflects disturbed proliferation, survival, or differentiation of epithelial stem cell-derived cells in hair follicles.

paragraphs.text: In 25 individuals with Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair, Cordeddu et al. (2009) identified a heterozygous 4A-G transition in the SHOC2 gene, resulting in a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution. Four were found among 96 mutation-negative individuals with Noonan syndrome and 21 among 410 mutation-negative individuals with Noonan syndrome or a related phenotype. The mutation was de novo in all families in which parental DNA was available. The mutation introduced an N-myristoylation site. This led to myristoylation of SHOC2, targeting of the protein to the plasma membrane, impaired nuclear translocation after growth factor stimulation, and cell type-specific enhancement of MAPK activation.

paragraphs.text: Hannig et al. (2014) used Rasopathy gene panel sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.519G-A transition in the SHOC2 gene, resulting in a met173-to-ile (M173I) substitution. The proband was a 5-year-old girl of European ancestry with macrocephaly, ptosis, nystagmus, optic nerve hypoplasia, and sparse, slow-growing hair that was not loose. Her father, who had intellectual disability, sparse hair, and clubbed nails, also carried the variant. The variant was not found in 6,500 asymptomatic individuals. In SHOC2-depleted Cos1 cells, the mutant restored EGF-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation to only about 10% above basal levels. It bound PP1c poorly and produced only a mild increase in RAF-1 Ser338 phosphorylation. Protein stability, subcellular localization, and complex formation with M-RAS and RAF-1 were unaffected.
